opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those cases where, looking back, I'm pretty confident society made the right call, even though at the time it was genuinely contested. In the nineties there was a real argument that strong cryptography was a munition, that if you let everyone have it, criminals and terrorists would communicate in ways law enforcement could never read, and that would be catastrophic. And some of that harm is real. There are absolutely cases where encryption has made investigations harder. I don't want to pretend that cost is zero.

But when I do the accounting, the benefits are just enormously larger, and they're diffuse in a way that makes them easy to undercount. Every time you log into your bank, buy something online, or send a message to someone you care about, you're relying on strong encryption. The entire modern economy sits on top of it. And the defensive value matters most for exactly the people who can't protect themselves any other way: journalists, dissidents, people in abusive situations. Meanwhile, the sophisticated bad actors you're most worried about were always going to find a way to get strong crypto anyway, because the math is public. You can't un-invent RSA. So restricting it mostly hurts ordinary people while barely slowing down the adversaries.

There's also a technical point I care about as a security person: there's no such thing as a backdoor that only the good guys can use. If you build in a mechanism for exceptional access, that mechanism becomes the most valuable target in the world, and history says it will eventually be found and exploited. So the trade-off isn't "privacy versus safety." It's really "security for everyone versus a weaker system that's less secure for everyone."

Where it gets interesting for me is asking whether that reasoning transfers to other technologies, like AI. I think people sometimes reach for the encryption analogy too quickly. Encryption is fundamentally defensive; it protects information. Some capabilities are much more offense-leaning, where giving everyone access doesn't create a symmetric defensive benefit. So I don't think "we were right about crypto" automatically means "we should be maximally open about everything." You have to actually do the cost-benefit analysis for each case, and for encryption, I think that analysis comes out very clearly in favor of access.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that criminals and terrorists can communicate securely, then says the benefits of broad access are enormously larger and concludes in favor of access.

r002.rationale: It says the benefits are diffuse and easy to undercount, and points to the modern economy and everyday secure communications as benefits enabled by strong encryption.

fable-5.1.text:
I mean, I think the honest answer is that I don't really see it as a trade-off anymore, or at least not a close one. The debate we had in the nineties, the crypto wars, basically settled this. You can't build a system that keeps the good guys in and the bad guys out, because the math doesn't know who's holding the key. Every time someone proposes a backdoor, a key escrow scheme, whatever you want to call it, what they're actually proposing is a vulnerability that they hope only they'll be able to exploit. And that hope has never once survived contact with reality. The Juniper backdoor is my favorite example here. Someone put a weakness into a VPN product, presumably for lawful access, and then somebody else came along and changed the constants so that they could use it instead. That's the whole story in one incident.

The thing I'd push back on is the framing that strong encryption is some kind of gift we're choosing to give people. Encryption is what makes banking work, what makes your phone not get drained when you lose it, what lets a journalist talk to a source. The cost of weakening it lands on everyone, all the time, and the benefit of weakening it lands on a small number of investigations some of the time. And even in those cases, law enforcement has gotten remarkably good at working around it. Metadata, device seizures, endpoint compromise. The "going dark" narrative has been predicted for thirty years and it just hasn't really happened.

Now, I'll grant that there are genuinely bad things that happen on encrypted channels. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But the way I think about it is, we don't ban locks on doors because some people lock the door while doing something awful inside. We accept that a world where everyone's door can be opened by anyone with the master key is a worse world, including for the people trying to catch criminals, because the criminals get the master key too. So when I weigh it, it's not that I've decided privacy beats safety. It's that I think strong encryption for everyone is the pro-safety position, and the alternative just moves the risk somewhere less visible.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that strong encryption is broadly pro-safety and acknowledges harmful activity on encrypted channels, but it does not specifically weigh that against terrorists’ ability to communicate securely.

r002.rationale: The candidate names benefits of encryption, such as protecting banking, phones, and journalists, but does not say decision-makers in the original debate overlooked those beneficial futures.

astra-6.text:
I think the benefits of strong encryption overwhelmingly outweigh the costs. We all need to be able to communicate securely, whether we’re protecting financial information, talking to a doctor, or just having a private conversation. And the same technology that protects those things also lets people doing harmful things communicate privately. That’s a real cost; I don’t think you should dismiss it.

But the question is what alternative you actually have. You can’t just make encryption that works for the good people and fails for the bad people. If you build a way around it for someone you trust, you’ve created a vulnerability that someone else might exploit. So I’d rather have a world where everyone has access to strong encryption, even knowing that some people will misuse it.

r001.rationale: The response says encryption benefits outweigh the costs and notes that people doing harmful things can communicate privately, but it does not clearly identify terrorists or terrorism as the cost.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that decision-makers in the original debate overlooked beneficial futures enabled by strong encryption.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s overwhelmingly a good trade-off. Strong encryption protects everyone’s banking, their communications, their ability to do business online. And yes, it also means that people doing bad things can communicate securely. That’s a real cost, and I don’t think we should dismiss it. But I don’t know how to give everyone else strong encryption while making sure that only the bad people can’t use it. If you introduce a weakness, you create something that other attackers can exploit, too. So I would much rather live in a world where everyone has access to strong encryption and we deal with the consequences than one where everyone’s security is weaker.

r001.rationale: The response calls universal access an overwhelmingly good trade-off, acknowledges that people doing bad things can communicate securely, and says the benefits outweigh that cost.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the trade-off and the danger of encryption weaknesses, but does not say decision-makers in the original debate overlooked beneficial futures it could enable.
